grammar.name: Correlative conjunctions (not only...but also)

grammar.tip: Remember: if 'not only' is at the start of the sentence, you must invert the subject and verb. If it is in the middle, you do not.

grammar.name: Inversion after negative adverbials

grammar.name: Inversion in formal conditionals

grammar.tip: Use this pattern only in formal writing. Never use 'if' and the inverted word order together in the same sentence.

grammar.tip: Do not overuse this. A paragraph full of abstract nouns becomes hard to read, so balance it with clearer, simpler sentences too.

grammar.name: Ellipsis and substitution for cohesion
grammar.rule: This leaves out or replaces a word that was already used earlier in the sentence. It avoids repeating yourself and helps your writing flow better.
grammar.formula: ..., and so + auxiliary + subject | auxiliary + not (omitting the repeated verb phrase)
grammar.example: Older generations remain cautious about sport and recreation, and so, increasingly, do younger ones.
grammar.tip: Only leave out a word when the reader can easily guess it from context. If it is not clear, the sentence becomes confusing instead of smoother.

grammar.name: Proportional comparatives (the...the...)
grammar.rule: This shows a direct link between two things that change together — when one increases or decreases, so does the other.
grammar.formula: The + comparative + clause, the + comparative + clause
grammar.example: The more attention sport and recreation receives in public debate, the greater the pressure on lawmakers to respond.
grammar.tip: Keep both halves of the sentence grammatically the same. If they do not match, the sentence sounds wrong.

grammar.name: Modal perfect for past speculation
grammar.rule: This shows how certain or uncertain you are about something in the past. You use a modal verb followed by 'have + past participle'.
grammar.example: The delay in addressing sport and recreation must have resulted from competing political priorities.
grammar.tip: Choose the modal verb carefully. 'Must have' shows you are almost sure. 'Might have' or 'could have' shows it is just possible.

grammar.name: Correlative conjunctions (not only...but also)
grammar.rule: This connects two balanced ideas using a pair of linking words. When 'not only' starts the sentence, it triggers inversion in that clause.
grammar.formula: Not only + [inverted clause], but + subject + also + verb
grammar.example: Not only does sport and recreation affect the economy, but it also reshapes everyday social behaviour.
grammar.tip: Remember: if 'not only' is at the start of the sentence, you must invert the subject and verb. If it is in the middle, you do not.
